short: Meditation: an unbroken flow of attention toward one object.
beginner: Dhyana means meditation: letting attention rest on one thing steadily instead of jumping around. Almost every Indian tradition practises it, but each has a different idea of what it is for.
what: Dhyana is sustained, continuous attention. In Patanjali's Yoga it is the seventh limb, following concentration (dharana) and leading to absorption (samadhi). The Gita's sixth chapter describes a meditator's seat, posture and the steadying of a restless mind. In Buddhism the related term (Pali jhana) names a series of meditative absorptions; the word travelled through Chinese chan to Japanese zen.
scholar: YS 3.1–3 defines dharana, dhyana and samadhi as a graded series (together samyama). Buddhist abhidharma lists four form jhanas with specific factors (vitakka, vicara, piti, sukha, ekaggata). In the Gita, dhyana-yoga (ch. 6) is one discipline among karma, jnana and bhakti; Sadhak Sanjivani reads the goal of meditation as fixing the mind on God and ceasing to dwell on anything else.

perspectives.view: The seventh limb: a continuous flow of cognition toward the chosen object, which matures into samadhi.
A set of absorptions (jhanas) that calm and unify the mind; in most Buddhist schools they support insight but are not liberation by themselves.

Meditation (upasana, nididhyasana) helps assimilate what is learned from scripture. Advaita treats nididhyasana as dwelling on the Self already taught; theistic Vedanta treats meditation as loving remembrance of God.
Right meditation (dharma-dhyana, shukla-dhyana) is part of internal austerity that burns away karmic matter; agitated or angry brooding is counted as harmful meditation.
Meditative remembrance (simran) on the Name is central, practised within household life rather than in withdrawal.
